analysis.one_liner: Gives database companies a 25-year exclusive right over compiled facts and data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after its May 1996 introduction it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a brand-new kind of property right in databases — collections of facts like phone listings, legal records, or scientific data. Unlike copyright, which protects creative expression but not facts, this would have given database owners 25 years of legal control over the information itself. Copying or reusing a substantial part of a database without permission would have been a civil violation, and commercial piracy could bring prison time of up to five years. Selling or building tools to get around database protections would also have been illegal.
analysis.who_benefits: Database owners — chiefly large commercial information companies that compile legal, financial, scientific, and directory data. They would gain a 25-year exclusive right (renewable whenever the database is updated in a commercially significant way) to control who can extract, reuse, or compete with their compilations, backed by injunctions, damages up to three times actual losses, and criminal penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Gives database makers an exclusive right lasting 25 years over the contents of any database built with substantial investment, protecting them against unauthorized extraction and reuse regardless of medium [S2][S3].
Backs that right with civil remedies — injunctions, impoundment, defendant's profits, actual damages up to treble, and attorney's fees — for the database owner [S3].
Adds criminal penalties for willful commercial violations: up to $250,000 and five years in prison, doubling to $500,000 and ten years for repeat offenders [S2][S3].

Bans manufacturing, distributing, or servicing tools whose primary purpose is to bypass database protection systems, and bans tampering with database management information, with statutory damages of $200 to $25,000 per violation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who reuses information: researchers and scientists analyzing data, libraries, journalists, and competing information services that build products on existing compilations. Because the bill covered databases whose contents were obtained from government sources [S3], publicly funded data could be locked up by the private company that compiled it, and end users would likely face higher prices for information services.

drawbacks.text: It creates a property right in facts themselves. Copyright has never protected facts, precisely so that information stays available for research, criticism, and new products; this bill would let a database owner control reuse of the underlying data for 25 years [S2][S3].
The protection effectively never expires. Any 'change of commercial significance' — including accumulated additions and updates — starts a fresh 25-year term for the resulting database [S2][S3].

The prohibited-use test is sweeping: reuse is barred if it competes 'in any market in which the database owner has a demonstrable interest or expectation in licensing,' or serves 'customers who might otherwise reasonably be expected to be customers for the database' — language that reaches far beyond actual piracy [S3].
The exception for lawful users is narrow: they may extract only 'insubstantial parts,' and even that carve-out can be overridden by the repeated-or-systematic-extraction prohibition [S3].
Databases whose contents come from government sources are covered, so data the public effectively paid for through public agencies could be fenced off by a private compiler [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the anti-circumvention ban and criminal penalties (up to ten years for repeat offenses) could be used against tinkerers, researchers, and small businesses, not just commercial pirates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The anti-piracy concern is real: compiling large databases takes serious investment, and digital copying makes theft cheap. But the remedy goes far beyond stopping piracy. Copyright already protects the creative arrangement of data, and contracts can govern access; this bill would add a 25-year, self-renewing exclusive right in facts themselves, with a 'potential market' test broad enough to block most competing uses, criminal penalties, and a ban on circumvention tools. The costs to research, competition, and access to public data outweigh the narrow piracy problem it solves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee in May 1996, and the committee never acted on it, so it simply expired when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Carlos Moorhead (R-CA) introduced the Database Investment and Intellectual Property Antipiracy Act of 1996 on May 23, 1996 [S1][S5].
It had five cosponsors — three Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on May 23, 1996, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — was ever taken [S5].
The 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, no new exclusive right in facts was created. Researchers, libraries, journalists, competing information services, and everyone who uses compiled data are better off than they would have been under the bill. Database publishers, which sought the protection, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Researchers and users of compiled data

for.name: Rep. Carlos J. Moorhead
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 23, 1996 and delivered introductory remarks [S1][S5].

for.name: Commercial database and information publishing industry
for.role: Industry seeking legal protection for compiled data
for.what_they_did: Sought a new U.S. legal right over database contents, a proposal the industry had long pursued; the bill's stated purpose is to 'promote investment' in databases.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S5].

against.name: Library, research, and scientific communities
against.what_they_did: Opposed creating exclusive property rights in facts, arguing such rights would restrict research and access to information.

sides.party_line_note: The only partisan evidence is the sponsor's list: a Republican sponsor with three Democratic and two Republican cosponsors; no vote was ever taken, so no party split on the merits is recorded [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Commercial database and information publishers (legal, financial, scientific, directory data)
industries.note: The bill would hand them a 25-year, effectively renewable exclusive right over compiled facts, enforceable with treble damages and criminal penalties. Their gain is the public's cost: higher prices and restricted reuse of data, including data originally obtained from government sources [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Competing information services and value-added data products
industries.note: Firms building competing products from existing compilations would face lawsuits under the broad 'potential market' test, since serving customers who 'might otherwise be expected' to buy the database would count as a violation [S3].

industries.industry: Universities, research libraries, and scientific publishing
industries.note: Scientific research depends on reusing data; the narrow 'insubstantial parts' exception would leave most systematic data reuse exposed to liability [S3].
